Choose the duplicate definition first: identical bytes, near-identical wording/pixels, or semantically similar content are different tasks. Exact hashing handles byte identity. MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity of shingles and LSH generates likely textual overlap candidates. SimHash approximates cosine similarity of weighted feature sets. Neural embeddings capture semantic similarity but may merge distinct documents discussing the same topic.

Use a candidate-generation stage followed by a stricter pairwise verification stage. For images use perceptual features robust to intended transforms; for video compare temporal frame/segment signatures rather than a single thumbnail. Store canonical IDs, versions, and deletion lineage, and retain reasons for merges so errors can be undone.

Tune thresholds on labeled pairs including hard nonduplicates and transformations. Avoid naive transitive closure when A resembles B and B resembles C but A does not resemble C. Evaluate precision/recall by duplicate type, cluster quality, throughput, and index freshness. Sharded LSH/ANN indexes improve scale but require careful handling of hot buckets and high-frequency boilerplate.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** MinHash collision probability equals Jaccard similarity of the represented sets; random-hyperplane sign agreement equals $1-\theta/\pi$ for angular similarity. These support candidate generation under different notions of similarity. Use stricter verification before merging records, and retain reversible cluster decisions because approximate similarity is not necessarily transitive. [3](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/33026.pdf) and [2](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/series/faiss/locality-sensitive-hashing/).
